title: min, abs, and round make numbers easier to read
when_to_show: When finding the minimum value in a list of numbers or reading the difference or the rounded result
body: min selects the smallest value, abs returns an absolute value, and round returns a rounded value. They do not mutate the input, but min([]) raises ValueError and binary floating-point rounding may differ from an intuitive decimal rule. Check input type, emptiness, and how the result is used.

title: `any` and `isinstance` are tools for checking conditions.
when_to_show: When checking whether any of the conditions in the list is true or verifying the type of a value
body: `any` and `isinstance` are commonly used tools for checking conditions. `any` evaluates the entire expression to `True` if any one of several conditions is `True`. For example, `any(x > 10 for x in nums)` checks whether there is at least one value greater than 10 in `nums`. `isinstance(value, int)` checks whether `value` is of the `int` data type. When reading code, look first at the loop condition inside `any` and determine which condition, if any, needs to be satisfied. `isinstance` frequently appears in input validation, function argument checks, and branching logic between strings and numbers. It’s best to view both not as functions that directly produce answers, but as decision-making tools that determine which path the next `if` statement will take. `any` asks, “Is there at least one?” while `isinstance` asks, “Is this value of the expected type?” The more complex the condition, the more stable the flow becomes when you rephrase it as these questions. This is particularly useful in code where value types can be mixed, such as with user input or JSON data. Think of them as filters that only pass values that meet the condition to the next step.
detail: `any` checks whether any of several conditions is true, while `isinstance` verifies that a value’s data type matches the expected type. Both are frequently used as decision-making tools that determine the flow of a conditional statement. When reading code, it helps to first paraphrase the loop condition inside `any` and the target value of `isinstance` into plain language to better understand the flow.

title: `startswith`, `endswith`, and `find` check the position and format of a string
when_to_show: When checking file names, prefixes, suffixes, and locations
body: `startswith`, `endswith`, and `find` are tools for checking the structure and position of a string. `startswith` returns `True` or `False` depending on whether a string begins with a specific character, and `endswith` returns `True` or `False` depending on whether it ends with a specific character. `find` returns the position where the target string first appears as a number; if it is not found, it returns -1. When reading code, note that `startswith` and `endswith` are often used directly in conditional statements, while `find` is frequently used to determine positions for slicing or branching decisions. For example, `filename.endswith(".json")` checks for a file extension, and `url.startswith("https://")` checks for a valid URL format. Code like `text.find("error") >= 0` can be interpreted as a flow to check whether a specific word is present. It is frequently used for file extension checks, URL filtering, prefix classification, log searches, and simple string parsing. The `if` statement often branches depending on whether the result of `find` is -1 or not. Therefore, you need to consider both the fact that the return value is a number and how it is compared in conditional statements.
detail: `startswith`, `endswith`, and `find` are functions that check the beginning, end, and position of a string. `startswith` and `endswith` return `True` or `False`, while `find` returns the position number or `-1`. In code that checks filenames, URLs, logs, or file extensions, you must verify how the return values are compared in conditional statements.

title: An f-string embeds a variable's value within a string
when_to_show: When outputting a string that contains variable values
body: An f-string is a syntax that naturally embeds variable values into a string. When you use curly braces ({}) within a string prefixed with an "f"—such as {name} or {count}—the current value of the variable or the result of a simple calculation is inserted in that position. When reading code, it’s easier to distinguish between characters that remain as-is within the quotes and parts that are evaluated within the curly braces. For example, `f"{user}, {score} points"` reads the current values of `user` and `score` to construct a single string. F-strings are frequently used in `print` output, log messages, filename generation, API response messages, and error messages. It’s important to note that the values at the moment the f-string is created are the ones that get inserted into the string. Even if the variables change afterward, the string that has already been created will not automatically update. Therefore, if the output differs from what you expected, you should first trace how the variable values changed before the f-string line. The curly braces can contain not only simple variables but also simple expressions. However, for overly complex calculations, it’s easier to read if you first assign the result to a variable outside the f-string.
detail: An f-string creates a new string by interpolating the current value of a variable into the string. It’s easier to understand if you separate the fixed text inside the quotes from the part that is evaluated within the curly braces. You should also note that even if the variable’s value changes after the f-string is created, the string that has already been generated will not automatically change.

title: `list.pop` removes a value from the list while retrieving it.
when_to_show: When retrieving the last value or a value at a specific position from a list
body: list.pop returns and removes the item at an index, using the last item when no index is supplied. An empty list or out-of-range index raises IndexError. Track the list before the call, the returned item, and the list afterward.

title: `setdefault` and `dict.pop` modify the state of the dictionary
when_to_show: When setting a default value in a dictionary or removing a key
body: Both `setdefault` and `dict.pop` are tools that can modify the state of a dictionary. `setdefault(key, default_value)` sets the default value if the key does not exist and returns that value. If the key already exists, it does not set the new default value but simply returns the existing value. This is why it’s often seen in the “create if it doesn’t exist, use the existing one if it does” pattern. `dict.pop(key)` removes the value associated with that key from the dictionary. Just like `pop` in a list, it returns a value, so you can store the retrieved value in another variable, such as `removed = data.pop("old")`. When reading code, you should check whether `setdefault` created a new key, whether `pop` removed a key, and whether the result is used in subsequent conditions or output. Since this pattern appears particularly frequently in code involving accumulative dictionaries, grouping dictionaries, option dictionaries, and cache cleanup, it’s a good idea to read the code by comparing the dictionary’s state before and after the operation. If you pass a default value to `pop`, it will return the default value instead of raising an error when the key does not exist. Therefore, you can interpret this code as performing both safe deletion and value retrieval simultaneously.
detail: `setdefault` sets a default value when a key does not exist, and `dict.pop` removes a key from the dictionary while retrieving its value. Since both operations can alter the state of the dictionary, you must check whether the key exists before and after execution. In code for grouping, accumulation, and option handling, both the return value and changes to the dictionary are important.

title: Distinguish between discard, intersection, difference, and set comprehension
when_to_show: When safely removing elements from a set or identifying similarities and differences
body: A set is a collection of unique values. While a list prioritizes order and position, a set focuses on which values are included and on removing duplicates. `discard` is a safe removal tool that removes a value without raising an error even if the value is absent. `intersection` finds the common values between two sets, while `difference` finds values present in one set but not in the other. A set comprehension is a syntax for creating a new set using loops and conditions, similar to a list comprehension. When reading code, it’s helpful to remember that a set is not a data structure designed to guarantee the order of results, but rather one that excels at “membership checks” and “set comparisons.” For example, the intersection of `allowed` and `used` represents the allowed items that have actually been used, while `required.difference(done)` can be interpreted as the items that have not yet been completed. This concept frequently appears in tasks such as removing duplicates, checking permissions, comparing tags, and finding missing items. The result of a set operation is usually a new set. Therefore, to minimize errors, you should pay close attention to whether the original set is being modified or if the new result is being stored in a variable.
detail: A set is a data type where membership and the removal of duplicates are more important than order. The `discard` method removes elements without causing an error, even if they are not present; `intersection` finds common values, and `difference` finds values present in only one set. A set comprehension creates a new set from values that satisfy a condition. You must distinguish between the original set and the new result.

title: `readline` and `readlines` read files line by line.
when_to_show: When looking at code that reads the first line or multiple lines from a file,
body: You’ll often encounter `readline` and `readlines` when creating a workflow to read a file line by line. While `read()` fetches the entire file as a single large string, `readline()` reads only one line from the current position and moves on to the next line. This makes them a natural choice for creating a “read one line, check it, and store only the necessary values” workflow within a loop. Since `readlines()` retrieves multiple lines as a list, it’s convenient for quickly reviewing configuration files or sample data that don’t contain many lines. When reading code, you should first determine whether the file is read all at once, whether a list of lines is created, or whether it is processed line by line in a loop. Since line break characters may remain at the end of a line, also check whether `strip()` or `rstrip()` is used in conjunction. It’s also worth remembering that `readlines()` can consume a lot of memory with large files, and reading line by line may be safer in such cases. In file-handling problems, the current read position is also important. If you want to read from the beginning again after reading once, you may need code to reopen the file or rewind the position.
detail: `readline` and `readlines` are frequently used in workflows that handle files line by line. `readline` reads one line at a time and advances the position, while `readlines` collects multiple lines into a list. Since the newline character at the end of each line may remain, you should also check whether `strip`-style processing is available and whether large files can be read all at once.

title: "global" indicates that the variable outside the function will be modified directly.
when_to_show: When you see code that modifies an outer variable from within a function
body: The `global` keyword indicates that you intend to directly modify a variable outside the function. At the beginner level, it’s more important to read code carefully than to use `global` frequently. If you write something like `count = count + 1` inside a function, Python typically treats `count` as a local variable within that function. However, if `global count` is present, it means the function intends to directly modify the outer `count`. When reading code, as soon as you see `global`, you should assume that the value of the outer variable may change even after the function has finished executing. While this might seem convenient in small examples, it becomes difficult to track where values have changed as the code grows. Therefore, whenever possible, it’s better to compare the code to a structure where a function returns a new value, and that value is then stored again outside the function. While `global` can be useful for quickly sharing configuration values, counters, or temporary states, it’s also a red flag that can make testing and debugging difficult. Therefore, when solving a problem and you see `global`, try writing down the values before and after the function call separately. This way, you won’t confuse what’s displayed on the screen with the actual stored state.
detail: The `global` keyword indicates that a variable outside the function will be modified directly within the function. Unlike the typical flow of local variables, the value of the outer variable may change after the function is called, so you must explicitly note the values before and after the call. If possible, compare this to a structure that returns a new value using `return`, and treat `global` as a warning sign.
